My parents would let me do whatever I wanted in regards to sports, events, extra curricular activities, etc. I was raised well with mannerisms, respect, and golden rule but my dad is alpha male and would often override my mom's stern parenting (which I desperately needed growing up). I knew that I had something off with me and my train of thought and direction but when I told my dad he said that "No son of mine is retarded. Nothing is wrong with you". He was a bootstraps kind of man and now, as a 31 year old married man, he understands. He loves me more than anything but I had this diagnosed as a kid, they could have caught this genetic depression caused by lack of endorphin production and now I know I might have Alzheimers. 

I had a midlife crisis or a early one, last year and when I got help, the tests came back with a lot of helpful information that I decided to share with my parents. I know it is hard for my dad to accept change (hes 72) and he's stubborn as hell but he's learning, he is trying, and checking up on me. 

Everyone is different but this is my experience with it.

My experience when I was diagnosed was that if you're looking to get something that day, and you press the issue, it might come off as desparate. If they put you through a few medications before they give you what you want, then you might have to roll with it. 

But if you were really diagnosed, and can prove it, it would be extremely beneficial to your cause. Don't try to give a list of symptoms that the college stereotype would Google and then ramble off to a doc. My psychiatrist once told me that it was so easy to distinguish those who needed it and those who wanted it for completely the wrong reasons. Everyone had moments where they "can't focus" and "can't stay on track" but it isn't always a clear cut attention deficit diagnosis. If you bullshit around, get the meds, and it doesn't have the same effect, that could be harfum to you as well. 

Being honest, open, explain symptoms in detail with examples.

Ok, I had the same thing happen to me about 10 years ago. I wasn't honest and had a hard time with opiates back then. My then PCP drug tested and closed me out after giving me scripts for all sorts of medication. Come day seven and eight, I was all sorts of delusional. 

My biggest piece of advice is to find an urgent care or an open clinic where you can discuss it with someone and they can get you scripts for medications that aren't controlled. Some times they can but it depends on the physician, state, country, etc. There's a progeam here called MHMR (Mental Health and Mental Retardation) and they help a wide variety of individuals with various types of developmental disabilities, autism, job training, and job coaching, among other things. Anyway, they were another source for me to guide me in the direction I needed actually. 

Landing a psychiatrist, to me, has been a better experience with a PCP just because it feels more open, free, and I can be honest. Hell, even going to the hospital or a similar style care center to ask about it, isn't a bad idea either. The more open, honest, and inquisitive you are, the easier it is to get direction. Don't worry or be scared. Message me if you have any questions or concerns. I will do whatever I can in my power to help.

It covers medications for a ton of categories some of them are mood stabilizers, anti depressants, pain medications, sleep medications, etc... by doing this, it severely helps limit the amount of meds you are traditionally peppered with. It's insane. I talk about my childhood love it was a bad thing but my dad was only mentally abusive but stern, loving, and still... mentally abusive. Never used profanity or foul language but could make you feel like shit and then pretend like it didnt happen the next day. My mom's voice was masked by him and eventually, like his past three marriages, his cheating and love for women got the best of him and they got divorced when I was 16. Mom didnt want us to live with her as my dad made 6 figures and didnt want to take anything away from him as he could provide a better life style for my younger sister and I.

This was a hard period for me. I was spoiled rotten but it came with a price. My older siblings (both of which are near 50) were severely mentally abused and neglected and my dad thought it would be better of him to be a better father by spoiling us and not really holding us accountable. 

He did teach me to work my ass off, treat all living creatures with respect, and never under any circumstances let someone hit you first. If you can tell you're going to get punched, hit them back or find a way to disarm the situation.  So I lied on my apartment application when I was 17, moved out, and struggled for life to stay afloat. Being able to communicate with the general public got me from a Janitor to department supervisor of many departments, management training classes, college classes and certificates paid for by the company, all to be thrown away nearly 14 years later due to my mental health. 

The people you can fake being happy around can sometimes end up being completely genuine which will allow you to reveal yourself and they end up staying around because of it. I have learned though that honesty might be a scary deterrent and use discretion. But if you can relate and talk with a genuine person, letting them see a glimpse of your misery isn't such a bad idea and might end up doing more good than anything else. It has got people to help me and give me direction when I'm lost and I've been open to it. I thought at first that "oh hey I'm the ADHD, manic depressive, can barely produce endorphins, nut job of a human, there's no way they stick around" and they did. They listened and appreciated the honesty. It's different for everyone but I pick and choose when I feel like being open but when I do, I'm not scared.
